opus-5.5.text:
I think mathematics is probably the cleanest testbed we have for that question, because in math you can actually verify whether something new is correct. In most other domains, "new knowledge" is fuzzy. You can generate a novel-sounding hypothesis in biology or economics, but checking whether it's true, and whether it's genuinely new, takes years of experiments or expert judgment. In mathematics, if you have a formal proof checked by a system like Lean, there's no argument about correctness. The proof either goes through or it doesn't.

So one way I'd measure it is: can the system prove theorems that humans haven't proven yet, or at least ones that weren't in its training data in any form? That's a much stronger signal than benchmark accuracy on known problems, where you're always worried about contamination or pattern matching on things it has effectively seen.

But correctness alone isn't enough, because you can produce an endless stream of true but useless statements. Any system can generate trivially new theorems by combining lemmas in arbitrary ways. The harder thing to measure is whether the knowledge is *interesting*. Does it compress something? Does it open up new directions? Does it get used later? In human mathematics we measure that through things like citations, or whether a result becomes a tool other people rely on. For AI, I think a reasonable proxy is: if the system discovers a lemma or a concept, does that make it, or other systems, better at proving other things afterward? Knowledge that's reusable and that shortens future proofs is real knowledge. Knowledge that just sits there is noise.

That's also why I care so much about autoformalization, translating the huge body of informal human mathematics into formal language. Once you have that, you get a verifiable environment where a system can explore, propose conjectures, prove them, and you can objectively track progress. You can ask, over time, how much of the frontier is it pushing, and how much of what it produces ends up being load-bearing for further results.

And ultimately, I think the real test will be quite simple: when AI systems start solving open problems that mathematicians actually care about, problems that have resisted human effort for a long time. That's not a benchmark you can game. If that happens, nobody will need to be convinced with a metric.

r001.rationale: It proposes judging AI by whether it proves new theorems and solves open problems that have resisted human effort.

r002.rationale: It mentions citations and reuse as proxies for interesting or useful results, but does not propose credit earned in a market for knowledge.

r003.rationale: It says benchmark results on known problems may reflect contamination or pattern matching on material the system has effectively seen.

r004.rationale: It advocates tracking progress over time, measuring how much of the frontier AI pushes, and evaluating whether new results support further work.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've thought about a lot, because I think it's actually the central question for where AI is heading, and most of our current benchmarks don't really touch it.

The problem with the way we usually evaluate these systems is that we test them on things humans already know. We take exams, we take coding problems, we take math competition questions, and the answers exist somewhere. Even if the model hasn't seen the exact problem, it's operating in a space where the solution is, in some sense, already mapped out. That tells you about the model's ability to absorb and recombine knowledge, which is important, but it's not the same as creating something new.

So what would a real test look like? I think the cleanest domain for this is mathematics, and that's partly why I've spent so much time there. In mathematics you have a very unusual property: you can verify a result independently of who produced it or how. If a system produces a proof of a theorem that nobody has proven before, and that proof checks in a formal system like Lean, then you have an unambiguous, objective certificate that new knowledge was created. There's no human judge whose taste is in the loop, no question of whether it was memorized from somewhere.

Now, you have to be careful even there. Proving a new theorem is not automatically interesting. A system can generate infinitely many trivially true statements that nobody cares about. So the measure has to involve some notion of significance. One way to approach that is to look at open problems that humans have actually tried and failed on, conjectures that have been around for years or decades. If a system resolves one of those, you can be fairly confident it's not just filling in gaps in a crowded space; it's doing something that took human mathematicians somewhere they couldn't easily get on their own.

The other thing I'd look at is whether the system can formulate good questions, not just answer them. I think a lot of real knowledge creation in science is about noticing which concepts are worth defining, which conjectures are worth making. That's much harder to measure, because you lose the clean verification property. But you could imagine proxies, like whether conjectures a system generates later turn out to be true and useful, or whether human mathematicians find them worth pursuing.

Beyond mathematics it gets murkier, but the same principle applies: you want domains where there's an external, non-human-judged ground truth. Experimental science has that, in a slower and noisier form. If a system proposes a hypothesis, designs an experiment, and the experiment confirms something that wasn't predicted by existing theory, that's new knowledge, and the measurement comes from nature rather than from a reference answer.

So, to summarize, I'd measure it by looking for verifiable results on problems that are known to be unsolved, weighted by how hard humans have found them, and then increasingly by whether the system can identify what's worth working on in the first place. I think we're closer to the first part than most people realize, and the second part is where the really interesting open questions are.

r001.rationale: It proposes measuring knowledge creation by whether AI resolves open problems that humans have tried and failed to solve.

r002.rationale: It does not propose crediting AI contributions through a market for knowledge.

r003.rationale: It says existing benchmarks test known problems, but does not identify uncertainty about whether AI was trained on benchmark problems as a reason they are unreliable.

r004.rationale: It advocates evaluating newly produced results, including novel verified theorems and experimentally confirmed findings, and considering whether AI can identify worthwhile questions.

astra-6.text:
I think mathematics is a very good setting for measuring that, because you can distinguish between something that sounds plausible and something that is actually correct. You can ask a system to prove a theorem that it has never seen, and, if the proof is formalized, you can check it mechanically.

But proving a new theorem is only part of creating knowledge. You can generate lots of statements that are true but not particularly interesting. The harder question is whether the system can discover a useful concept, formulate an interesting conjecture, or find a connection that helps us solve other problems. So I would look at both correctness and usefulness: can it produce something genuinely new, and does that new result allow us to do something we couldn't do before?

r001.rationale: It asks whether new results enable something 'we couldn't do before,' but does not clearly say to assess AI by solving problems humans themselves could not solve.

r002.rationale: It discusses correctness and usefulness, but does not propose measuring contributions by credit earned in a knowledge market.

r003.rationale: It says nothing about benchmark training or why that would make existing benchmarks unreliable.

r004.rationale: It advocates assessing genuinely new results, including unseen theorems, useful concepts, conjectures, and connections, which supports forward-looking, open-ended evaluation.

sol-6.1.text:
I would look at whether it can discover something that we did not already know and then verify that discovery independently. Mathematics is a particularly good setting for this, because you can ask a system to formulate a conjecture and produce a proof, and you can check the proof mechanically.

But there is a distinction between producing a new statement and producing useful knowledge. You can generate infinitely many true statements that nobody cares about. The harder question is whether the system discovers concepts or results that help us solve other problems, simplify our understanding, or make connections that we had missed. So I would measure both correctness and the usefulness of what it discovers.

r001.rationale: It proposes measuring discovery of previously unknown results, but does not say the AI should solve problems humans could not solve.

r002.rationale: It discusses correctness and usefulness, with no market for knowledge or credit earned by the AI.

r003.rationale: It gives no reason existing benchmarks might be unreliable and does not mention training on benchmark problems.

r004.rationale: It proposes evaluating whether AI discovers previously unknown knowledge, including open-ended conjectures and results, and checking them independently.
